source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: SHY says sleep is the price of plasticity. Learning in wake raises net synaptic strength. Strong synapses cost energy, cut signal-to-noise and saturate learning. Sleep renormalizes strength by activity-dependent down-selection.
numbers: Core claims: (i) learning mainly by potentiation in wake, (ii) no potentiation in sleep, (iii) renormalization in sleep. Brain uses up to 25% of body glucose at 2% of body mass.
limits: A theory paper plus review. SHY does not rule out some depression in wake or some potentiation in sleep. The balance holds over the 24 h cycle.
agent_relevance: Maps to a lesson store: add freely while working (wake), then run a separate offline pass that shrinks everything and keeps what is strong or well connected.
quote: SHY proposes that the fundamental function of sleep is the restoration of synaptic homeostasis

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: Why renormalize in sleep and not in wake: wake input is a narrow, biased sample (the plasticity-stability dilemma). Sleep spontaneous activity samples the brain's whole stored knowledge, so depression can be fair to old memories.
numbers: Example in the paper: after a day with a new acquaintance, weakening unused synapses in wake would keep the new person and lose old friends.
limits: Conceptual argument, not directly tested as such.
agent_relevance: Pruning lessons must be judged against the whole lesson library, not only the last task. Do not prune on recency of the current session.

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: Molecular and electrophysiological evidence: GluA1-AMPAR levels are higher after wake than after sleep in rat cortex. In humans a TMS evoked-response slope rises over 18 h of wake and returns to baseline after recovery sleep.
numbers: GluA1 AMPARs 30-40% higher after wake than sleep (Vyazovskiy 2008, rats). Human frontal TMS slope up over 18 h wake, back to baseline after one night (Huber 2012).
limits: Markers are indirect. Evoked slope can also move with neuromodulator-driven excitability.
agent_relevance: An agent can log a strength score per lesson that rises with use and decays in a rest pass.

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: Structural evidence in flies and mice: synapse number or spine density rises with wake and falls with sleep. In adult mice spine turnover is limited, so adult homeostasis is likely by strength, not number.
numbers: Drosophila VS1 neuron: spines rise after 12 h enriched wake, fall only if flies sleep (Bushey 2011). Adolescent mice: net spine gain in wake, net loss in sleep (Maret 2011; Yang & Gan 2012 in 3-week-old mice). Adult mice: no sleep/wake spine effect.
limits: Age dependent: adolescent and juvenile animals show the structural effect, adults do not.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: pruning pressure is strongest when the store grew fast, weaker in a mature stable store.

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: Contradicting result noted in the review: in head-restrained cats, evoked cortical responses rose after sleep, not fell.
numbers: Chauvette 2012: effect after as little as 10 min of sleep, saturating after two short sleep episodes. Review authors argue it reflects sleep inertia (hyperpolarized membrane).
limits: Species and method difference; contested interpretation.
agent_relevance: Evidence on the direction of sleep change is not unanimous; make the prune pass reversible (archive, do not delete).

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: Slow wave activity (SWA, 0.5-4.5 Hz) marks sleep need and also acts as effector: stronger synapses give more synchrony and more SWA, SWA depresses synapses, so the process is self-limiting.
numbers: Control loop (Olcese 2010): depression rate proportional to firing/synchrony, so SWA decline in sleep is exponential and self-limiting. Suppressing SWA in the first 3 h of sleep prevents its decline (Dijk 1987). Local SWA rises after right-parietal learning (Huber 2004), falls after arm immobilization (Huber 2006).
limits: Some studies with other protocols failed to detect local SWA changes (Hanlon 2011).
agent_relevance: A prune pass should be self-limiting: the more the store has grown, the more it prunes; it stops at baseline. Use a proportional rule, not a fixed cut.

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: Three computer rules for down-selection: proportional downscaling with a floor (Hill 2008); STDP-like rule where strong synapses depress less (Olcese 2010); protection from depression for synapses that fire together in sleep (Hashmi/Nere 2013).
numbers: In all models the result is competitive down-selection: some synapses end less effective than others and signal-to-noise rises.
limits: Special case: a neuron with all inputs from one source cannot compete, so down-selection fails.
agent_relevance: Menu for lesson pruning: (1) multiplicative decay with floor, (2) decay scaled inversely to strength, (3) decay unless the lesson was co-used with other strong lessons.

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: Overtraining prediction: extra potentiation in wake or reactivation-potentiation in sleep lowers signal-to-noise and recall in the model, because noise synapses get potentiated too. Human visual texture task agrees: performance falls with overtraining and does not recover after sleep.
numbers: Models: extra wake or sleep potentiation lowered S/N and recall. Human data: Censor & Sagi 2008/2009 texture discrimination.
limits: Model-level and indirect behavioral support.
agent_relevance: Warning: re-reinforcing every lesson ('more rehearsal') may make the store worse by boosting noise lessons equally.

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: Behavioral benefits predicted: acquisition after sleep loss is impaired; boosting slow oscillations aids encoding.
numbers: Yoo 2007: episodic encoding impaired after sleep deprivation. Antonenko 2013: nap with slow-oscillation stimulation vs sham improved encoding of pictures, word pairs and word lists.
limits: Human behavioral studies; samples typically small.
agent_relevance: Supports a 'clear capacity before new learning' step: prune before the next task as well as after.

source: Nere, Hashmi, Cirelli, Tononi (2013) Sleep-dependent synaptic down-selection (I): modeling the benefits of sleep on memory consolidation and integration
finding: Spiking-network simulations. Wake: potentiate co-active synapses. Sleep: slow-oscillation reactivation with a 'protection from depression' rule. Down-selection raised procedural recall and signal-to-noise.
numbers: Procedural sequence A-B-C-D with 10% spurious sequences: after wake recall 80%, S/N 4; after one sleep 90%, S/N 9; later 95%, S/N 19. Extra wake potentiation: recall 20%, S/N 0. Potentiation in sleep: 25%, S/N 0.
limits: Small toy network; recall rule is 50% of group neurons active; no fit to real data.
agent_relevance: Pruning weak competitors lifts accuracy; strengthening everything collapses it. A number to beat in a lesson-store ablation.

source: Nere, Hashmi, Cirelli, Tononi (2013) Sleep-dependent synaptic down-selection (I): modeling the benefits of sleep on memory consolidation and integration
finding: Declarative paired-associate model: one sleep cycle lowers recall relative to just after training but is far better than staying awake. Cueing during sleep saves the cued items.
numbers: After training recall 87%, S/N 6; after sleep 75%, S/N 2; awake without sleep 53%, S/N 1; 10 wake/sleep cycles 94%, S/N 15. Cued pairs 95% (S/N 19) vs non-cued 75% (S/N 3); cued groups spent 8% more time in up-state.
limits: Recall first drops, then recovers over cycles; a single prune pass may look harmful short term.
agent_relevance: Prune passes may cost accuracy at first and pay back after several cycles; evaluate over multiple cycles. Cueing equals tagging lessons you expect to need.

source: Nere, Hashmi, Cirelli, Tononi (2013) Sleep-dependent synaptic down-selection (I): modeling the benefits of sleep on memory consolidation and integration
finding: Gist and integration: in a 3-level hierarchy, top-level (invariant) connections are protected by frequent reactivation while low-level detail synapses are depressed. New memories that fit old ones are protected; misfits are depressed.
numbers: Integrated new memory depressed only about 2% on average. Misfit memory: levels 1-2 depressed 28%, levels 2-3 11%. Unrelated old memories left inactive depress about 90% when potentiation and depression rates are equal.
limits: The 90% figure is a model artifact of equal rates, reported by authors as a caution about forgetting old friends.
agent_relevance: Keep lessons that are general or consistent with other kept lessons; drop narrow isolated ones. Guard against deleting old but unused lessons too fast.

source: Nere, Hashmi, Cirelli, Tononi (2013) Sleep-dependent synaptic down-selection (II): single-neuron level benefits for matching, selectivity, and specificity
finding: Single-neuron theory using information-theoretic 'Matching' between brain and environment: down-selection in sleep restores Matching after learning. Extra potentiation in wake, potentiation in sleep, or renormalization in wake all lower Matching.
numbers: Example neuron: after wake, firing rate 13% with World vs 11.1% with Chance (little selectivity); after down-selection the World rate fell to 11.2% and the Chance rate fell more.
limits: Toy neuron with few inputs.
agent_relevance: Formal case for separating learn mode from prune mode; pruning during the task itself is predicted worse than offline.

source: de Vivo, Bellesi, Marshall, Bushong, Ellisman, Tononi, Cirelli (2017) Ultrastructural evidence for synaptic scaling across the wake/sleep cycle (Science)
finding: Best direct test of SHY. 3D serial block-face electron microscopy of mouse motor (M1) and somatosensory (S1) layer 2. Axon-spine interface (ASI) was about 18% smaller after sleep than after both spontaneous and enforced wake.
numbers: 6,920 synapses analysed (168 dendrites, 8,427 spines); 3 groups of 4 mice (sleep, spontaneous wake at night, enforced wake by novel objects). Sleep vs SW -18.9% (p=0.001), vs EW -17.5% (p=0.003); SW vs EW -1.7% (p=0.957). Condition chi2=10.159, df=2, p=0.0062.
limits: Only 12 mice, adolescent, layer 2, two areas; sleep scored by video; a snapshot, so it cannot say which synapses were potentiated in wake.
agent_relevance: Gold-standard number: rest shrinks the store by about a fifth, not to zero. A prune of about 18% per cycle is biologically anchored.

source: de Vivo, Bellesi, Marshall, Bushong, Ellisman, Tononi, Cirelli (2017) Ultrastructural evidence for synaptic scaling across the wake/sleep cycle (Science)
finding: The shrinkage was selective and proportional to size (scaling). About 80% of synapses scaled; the largest ~20% did not. Only spines with recycling endosomes (vesicles, tubules, MVBs) scaled.
numbers: Small-medium synapses (80%): S vs SW -11.9% (p=0.0002), S vs EW -12.5%; large synapses: +0.7%, +2.0% (n.s.). Spines with endosomes: S vs SW -25.0% (p=0.00001), S vs EW -20.9%; without: -2.9%, -2.8% (n.s.). Spine head volume with endosomes -20.8% (p=0.0006).
limits: The small-vs-large pattern disagrees with Diering 2017 where large spines shrank most (per Tononi & Cirelli 2020).
agent_relevance: Two classes: a stable core that is protected and a plastic majority that is pruned. Tag heavily validated lessons as exempt from decay.

source: de Vivo, Bellesi, Marshall, Bushong, Ellisman, Tononi, Cirelli (2017) Ultrastructural evidence for synaptic scaling across the wake/sleep cycle (Science)
finding: Scaling depended on local crowding: less spiny dendrites downscaled most. Spine density itself did not change with sleep.
numbers: ASI fall largest in dendrites with lowest synaptic density: S vs SW -36.4%, S vs EW -25.3%; in dense dendrites +7.8% and -8.2%. Interaction p=0.038; synapse density by condition p=0.761. Monte Carlo: best-fit model was size-dependent selective scaling with >80% scaling.
limits: Interaction p-values are modest; one study.
agent_relevance: Pruning pressure can depend on neighbourhood: crowded topic areas keep entries, sparse areas thin out. A hint for per-cluster budgets.

source: Diering, Nirujogi, Roth, Worley, Pandey, Huganir (2017) Homer1a drives homeostatic scaling-down of excitatory synapses during sleep (Science)
finding: Molecular mechanism: during sleep Homer1a accumulates at the postsynaptic density, breaks the mGluR-Homer scaffold, and AMPA receptors (GluA1/GluA2) and their phosphorylation fall. This is absent in Homer1a knockout mice.
numbers: PSD proteomics: more than 4,500 PSD proteins and about 10,000 phosphopeptides; about 20% regulated across wake/sleep. PSD GluA1 and GluA2 lower in sleep; GluA3, NMDA subunits and PSD95 unchanged. Homer1a rises in the PSD in sleep while falling in whole forebrain.
limits: Mouse. The Homer1a gate is opened by adenosine and shut by noradrenaline; mild sleep deprivation by cage shaking did not block it but amphetamine did (per Tononi & Cirelli 2020).
agent_relevance: A two-key gate (arousal low AND need high) before pruning: do not prune while the agent is mid-task. Run the prune pass in an idle phase.

source: Cary & Turrigiano (2021) Stability of neocortical synapses across sleep and wake states during the critical period in rats (eLife)
finding: Failed test of SHY in young rats. mEPSC amplitudes in V1 and prefrontal cortex were stable across sleep-dense and wake-dense periods. Chronic thalamocortical responses in V1 were stable over prolonged sleep and wake.
numbers: Real-time sleep classification; mEPSC from L4 and L2/3 pyramidal neurons (V1 and PFC) in rats aged P25-P31; behavior in n=30 animals; chronic optogenetic monitoring n=4 animals.
limits: Juvenile critical-period animals; authors say generalization to the mature brain 'remains to be seen'. Different readouts (mEPSC, evoked response) from EM size.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence: downscaling is not universal. Treat the prune pass as testable: measure whether pruning helps, do not assume it.

source: Li, Ma, Yang, Gan et al. (2017) REM sleep selectively prunes and maintains new synapses in development and learning (Nat Neurosci)
finding: REM sleep prunes newly formed spines in mouse motor cortex and also strengthens and keeps some. This pruning makes room for later spine formation.
numbers: Abstract-level only: REM pruning of new spines requires dendritic calcium spikes. Numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Different stage (REM) and readout (spine formation) from SHY's NREM downscaling.
agent_relevance: Down-selection can be targeted: remove the NEW weak ones, keep selected new ones. Review newly added lessons first.

source: Yang, Lai, Cichon, Ma, Li, Zhang, Gan (2014) Sleep promotes branch-specific formation of dendritic spines after learning (Science)
finding: Counter-view to pure downscaling: sleep after motor learning promotes NEW spine formation on specific dendritic branches, and reactivation of learning-related neurons in NREM sleep is needed.
numbers: About 30% of apical tuft branches showed higher formation. Spine formation on high-formation branches in trained mice 15.3 +/- 1.3% vs 6.4 +/- 0.8% in untrained high-formation and 4.4 +/- 0.9% in low-formation branches (2.4 to 3.5 times, P<0.0001). 617 cells in 17 mice imaged; about 41% rose >50% in Ca2+ during running. REM deprivation (n=5) did not block it.
limits: Mouse M1; spine counts are not synaptic strength; SHY does not exclude circuit-specific strengthening.
agent_relevance: Alternative to blanket pruning: sleep also builds. A rest pass should both prune weak lessons and consolidate (rewrite, merge) the active ones.

source: Puentes-Mestril & Aton (2017) Linking network activity to synaptic plasticity during sleep: hypotheses and recent data (Front Syst Neurosci)
finding: Main critique of SHY: depending on prior experience, sleep can strengthen as well as weaken synapses. Proposes that several plasticity mechanisms operate in sleep.
numbers: Table: 1-2 h sleep vs sleep deprivation gave 5-10 fold higher pCaMKIIa, pERK, pSer831-GluA1 in cat V1 (Aton 2009); about 50% fewer new spines after ~7 h deprivation in mouse M1 (Yang 2014); about 20% lower CA1 spine density after 5 h deprivation (Havekes 2016); orientation response potentiation appears only after 6-12 h sleep in mouse V1.
limits: A review and hypothesis paper, not a replication; authors acknowledge the downscaling evidence.
agent_relevance: Competing hypothesis: pruning should depend on experience. Strengthen what was valuable, weaken what was low-value. Test both arms.

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2020) Sleep and synaptic down-selection (Eur J Neurosci)
finding: Authors answer critics and state two principles: spiking during sleep is required for down-selection, and renormalization spares neurons or synapses most active in sleep. The regulated variable is total synaptic strength, not firing rate.
numbers: Gulati 2017 rats: indirect units (90%) fell about 32% in task peak firing after sleep; direct units (67%) rose about 7%. Closed-loop optogenetic block of ON/UP states prevented both the gain and the drop; block in DOWN states did nothing.
limits: Own-group review, so interpretation is not neutral. They note de Vivo and Diering disagree on whether small or large synapses are targeted.
agent_relevance: Credit assignment idea: keep lessons causally tied to a verified success, drop correlated bystanders.

source: Gonzalez-Rueda, Pedrosa, Feord, Clopath, Paulsen (2018) Activity-dependent downscaling of subthreshold synaptic inputs during slow-wave-sleep-like activity in vivo (Neuron); read via Tononi & Cirelli 2020
finding: Under urethane anaesthesia (NREM-like), UP states bias plasticity toward depression; paired pre-post firing is protected. This supports the 'protection from depression' rule in vivo. Known only through the 2020 review.
numbers: Per the review: mean depression 63% (P16-P21) and 71% (P30-P50); strength never significantly increased in UP states.
limits: Anaesthesia model; mouse barrel cortex; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Concrete rule: decay unless co-activated with something that fired (a verified success).

source: Vyazovskiy et al. (2008) Molecular and electrophysiological evidence for net synaptic potentiation in wake and depression in sleep (Nat Neurosci); Huber et al. (2004, 2012)
finding: Founding electrophysiology: rat cortical evoked response slope rises with wake and falls with sleep, and the decline tracks the fall in SWA. Known only via the 2014 review.
numbers: Per review: GluA1 30-40% higher after wake; sleep decline of slope correlates with decline in SWA.
limits: Second-hand; original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: A measurable 'pressure' variable links to prune depth. Agent analogue: store growth since last prune.

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2003) Sleep and synaptic homeostasis: a hypothesis (Brain Res Bull); (2006) Sleep Med Rev
finding: Original statement of SHY, cited in the 2014 review. Predecessors named there: Crick & Mitchison 1983 reverse learning, Hinton et al. 1995 wake-sleep algorithm. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers extracted.
limits: Not opened; known only by citation in an opened review.
agent_relevance: Hinton's wake-sleep warning: strengthening fantasies in sleep is harmful, so offline passes should only weaken or protect verified items, never add unverified content.

source: Tadros, Krishnan, Ramyaa, Bazhenov (2022) Sleep-like unsupervised replay reduces catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks (Nat Commun)
finding: AI test of sleep ideas: after sequential training, a sleep-like phase (weights rescaled, Heaviside activations, noisy input, local Hebbian rule with potentiation and depression) recovers old tasks. It is replay-based, not pure downscaling.
numbers: CUB-200 baseline after two tasks: first task 5%, second task 95%; after a second sleep period overall accuracy on both tasks 90%. Also tested on MNIST, Fashion MNIST, CIFAR10.
limits: Small vision networks, not a language model; depression is part of the Hebbian rule so it is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Closest ANN evidence: an offline unsupervised pass can restore overwritten old knowledge. No LLM test found this session (arXiv search was rate-limited).

source: Bazhenov group (2022) Sleep prevents catastrophic forgetting in spiking neural networks by forming a joint synaptic weight representation (PLoS Comput Biol)
finding: Spiking network: new-task training moves weights off the old-task manifold. Interleaved offline reactivation keeps weights near the old manifold while converging toward the intersection of old and new tasks.
numbers: Control: freezing 1% of Task-1 relevant weights let Task 2 be learned but did not preserve Task 1.
limits: Single toy foraging task; no language data.
agent_relevance: Protecting a few important items is not enough; offline reconciliation of old and new is needed.

source: Tononi & Cirelli (2014) Sleep and the price of plasticity (Neuron review)
finding: Authors list limits of their own markers: in vitro mEPSC may not mirror in vivo; structure does not equal efficacy; no study had tagged individual synapses through a specific learning task and the following sleep.
numbers: Most cited studies had no explicit training, only staying awake.
limits: Self-stated limits.
agent_relevance: We can log per-lesson use and outcome, unlike neuroscience, so we can test down-selection at the single-item level.
